Chapter 6: Building Decision Groups — The Power of Constructive Dissent.
So, once you’ve got the basics of making decisions on your own, the next step is learning how to tap into the collective wisdom of a group.
Now, it’s easy to think the best teams are the ones who always agree with each other, right? But actually, the most effective decision groups are the ones where people are encouraged to disagree—where it’s not just allowed, but expected, to push back, challenge assumptions, and ask the hard questions.
At the center of a strong decision group is something called psychological safety. What does that really mean? It’s all about trust. Folks need to feel confident that if they raise a concern, or throw out a different point of view, they won’t get mocked or shut out. That kind of safety lets people speak up, share ideas, and, most importantly, uncover those hidden risks that might otherwise slip through the cracks.
Imagine a decision group as a crew of navigators steering a ship through foggy waters. Each person has their own vantage point. By sharing what they see—and what they worry about—the team can steer clear of hidden dangers and find the best route ahead.
Want to make your group decisions really work? Here are some tried-and-true approaches you can use:
Assign a “devil’s advocate.” Give someone the official job of questioning the popular opinion. And don’t let it be the same person every time—switch it up, so everyone gets to flex those critical thinking muscles.
Try running a pre-mortem. Picture this: before you lock in a decision, ask the team, “If this ends up failing, what’s most likely to have gone wrong?” It sounds simple, but it’s a powerful way to spot weak spots early.
Reward candor. When someone speaks up with a tough question or points out a flaw, let them know you appreciate it. A simple thank-you—especially in front of the group—goes a long way.
And don’t forget to document dissent. Keep a record of disagreements and the reasons behind them. That way, whether things go smoothly or not, there are lessons you can learn for next time.
Here’s how this plays out in the real world: imagine a product development team that holds regular “red team” sessions. In these meetings, a few folks are assigned to poke holes in the current plan, actively searching for weaknesses. Not only does this help the team catch problems early, but it also builds a culture where critical thinking is just as valued as being agreeable.
So, when you create space for constructive dissent, you help your group sidestep the trap of groupthink. Decisions become stronger, more resilient, and way more informed. And isn’t that what we’re all aiming for?
